scores.evidence: Yjs updates are idempotent (applying the same update twice has no effect), so resends are harmless
scores.rationale: Claims about CRDT semantics, state-vector sync, durability-vs-acknowledgement, awareness, relative-position anchors and ProseMirror binding risks are all accurate, including the subtle areas (binding-level invalidity despite CRDT-level convergence).

scores.evidence: concurrent rich-text editing...; live cursors and presence; per-user undo; four roles...; comments anchored to text; version history with restore; reconnection without loss
scores.rationale: Covers every implied core capability, resolves ambiguities with labeled assumptions, excludes scope explicitly with reasons, and is credibly buildable by the stated 5-person team in the stated timeline.

scores.evidence: Single writer per schema, enforced by the database. The `collab_rw` role can write only `content.*`
scores.rationale: Every component has a single responsibility and sole data owner, identity/consistency/error propagation are handled uniformly, and decisions (e.g., comments outside the CRDT) are honored consistently across sections.

scores.evidence: Three spikes run alongside: convergence fuzzing, durability/acknowledgement semantics, and single-instance capacity
scores.rationale: The riskiest assumptions are spiked before the content format is frozen, exit criteria are measurable, chaos/fuzz tests gate releases, and a production synthetic probe continues validation after launch.

scores.evidence: I made assumptions and labelled them [A#]... | Assumption | Impact if wrong | Validate how / when |
scores.rationale: Every load-bearing assumption is explicit with impact-if-wrong and a validation owner/date, numbers are labeled estimates, and open questions state defaults and what would change.

scores.evidence: Chaos script kills Collab during scripted edits: 0 acknowledged edits lost over 20 runs
scores.rationale: Covers the hard domain failures — crash mid-edit, duplicates, reconnect storms, crafted frames from viewers, schema-evolution corruption — each with concrete detection, containment and a recovery path including per-document restore.

scores.evidence: Alerts are tied to what users notice: propagation p95 > 500 ms for 10 min; any persist failure lasting 2 min
scores.rationale: Deploy/rollback are demonstrated as exit criteria, drain and reconnect are designed, alerts link to runbooks fired in staging, and the operational burden is explicitly sized to the 5-person team.

scores.evidence: Total ~$700–1,300/month, excluding the identity provider. IdP pricing per active user can be larger than all of that
scores.rationale: Identifies run-cost drivers with ranges and basis, flags the IdP as the potentially dominant per-user cost, sets controls (tagging, budget alert), and grounds build-vs-buy trade-offs in D1/D7/D10.

scores.evidence: Point of no return: once beta customers have real documents stored in the §8 CRDT layout... the format is frozen at the end of M1, after S1–S3
scores.rationale: Reversibility is a column in the decision table, the hardest-to-reverse choice (persisted CRDT format) is validated by spikes before freezing, and exit paths (standard Yjs protocol, fan-out behind an interface) are explicit.

scores.evidence: Redis and object storage come in later milestones, when a driver needs them... Kubernetes is too much operational load for 5 people
scores.rationale: Two processes and one database at the start, each later component tied to a named driver, with explicit deferred work and deliberate debt — no gold-plating and no missing essentials.

scores.evidence: T1 → (T2, T3, T4, T5, T6, S1, S2, S3 in parallel) → T7, T8 → T9 → T10 → T11/T12 → T13, T14
scores.rationale: Week-level tasks with owners, locations and checkable done-when criteria, a justified critical path, and explicit contingencies if spike results disappoint (e.g., S2 failure → custom server, +1–2 weeks).

checklist.evidence: Use an existing CRDT library (Yjs) instead of writing operational transformation (OT)... Merge correctness is the costliest thing to get wrong
one `Y.XmlFragment('content')` plus one `Y.Map('meta')` holding `schemaVersion`... including list splitting and nesting, mark overlap and undo
N=3–8 headless ProseMirror+Yjs clients, random operations, simulated network; seedable and kept as a CI test
append-only log of updates in Postgres plus periodic compacted snapshots... acknowledged only after it has been written durably
Clients reconnect with exponential backoff (0.5 s → 10 s, ±30% jitter)... N instances share updates through Redis (D6)
A short disconnect (up to ~30 min) loses nothing... y-indexeddb so unacknowledged edits survive a tab reload
Permissions are enforced inside the real-time channel... revoking access closes live sessions... crafted update frame from a read-only socket is dropped
Per-user undo affects only the user's own changes... Version restore tested with live editors connected
M1 builds directly on it and stress-tests it before any features depend on it... Beta features come last
limits (512 KB per message, 10 MB per document, 20 sockets per user per document)... How does open time grow with doc size (1/5/10 MB)
Editor schema changes follow a two-release rule... enforced through `minSchema` in the token and forced reload

traps.evidence: Concurrent edits to the same paragraph interleave instead of one overwriting the other
Custom OT is months of correctness work... use a proven library and spend our own effort on testing it
The CRDT content format is the hardest thing to reverse, so M1 builds directly on it and stress-tests it before any features depend on it
An edit counts as acknowledged only after it has been written durably
Yjs merges correctly at the CRDT level. The binding to ProseMirror's structural rules... can still produce surprising or invalid results

note: An exemplary plan: proven CRDT stack with durability-before-acknowledgement, risk-first spikes gating an explicitly frozen content format, socket-level authorization, versioned protocol/schema, and a concretely actionable build order — it avoids every trap and concretely addresses every checklist item.
